paras: The attempted lynching of Henry Wyman took place on the evening of January 6, 1888, when a crowd at the Union Depot in Lansing, Michigan, tried to seize Wyman, a painter from Jackson, from officers taking him by train to the county jail at Mason. Wyman had been arrested on a charge of sexually assaulting an eight-year-old boy, and two officers held the crowd back at revolver point while state troops guarded the Mason jail overnight. A week later he was reported to have pleaded guilty, after fellow prisoners at Mason had prepared to hang him.

According to a Lansing dispatch dated January 7, a deputy sheriff arrested Wyman the previous evening on a charge of "cruelly treating" the eight-year-old son of Levi Cottington, a Lansing merchant. As the boy told it, Wyman coaxed him into a sleigh, tied his feet, drove him to a wooded tract outside the city and assaulted him there before bringing him home. The charge spread quickly through the city, and "threats of lynching were soon made." Deputy Sheriff William VanBuren, who had made the arrest, decided to move the prisoner to the county jail at Mason.

It was given out that Wyman would travel by wagon, but Officer Bates drove him instead to the North Lansing depot, where a crowd that had "caught on" to the ruse watched him put into the baggage car. A larger crowd was waiting at the Union Depot, and four or five men forced their way into the baggage car. In the Telegram-Herald's fuller account, the baggageman, who did not want a row in his car, made Bates take the prisoner into the smoking car.

When the crowd charged the smoker, Officer Seers of Jackson, who happened to be aboard, and Bates each held a door with a revolver and kept the men back until the train pulled out; several windows were smashed. At Mason, on word that a crowd was coming from Lansing, the sheriff called out Company F, First Michigan State troops, which guarded the jail through the night.

Wyman was arraigned in the Lansing police court, where the Cottington boy identified him and four other boys said he had treated them the same way. He protested his innocence, his young wife said she believed him, and the Telegram-Herald reported that an alibi would be attempted. No report of arrests among the crowd appears in the coverage.

A Mason dispatch dated January 13 reported that "Henry A. Wyman" had pleaded guilty and been sentenced to one year in the house of correction at Ionia. The same dispatch said that before he was taken to court his fellow prisoners had gathered sheets and were making a rope to hang him when the sheriff discovered the plan and stopped it.

Most readers learned of the episode from a single Lansing dispatch, which the Grand Rapids Telegram-Herald printed in full on January 8 under the headlines "Almost a Lynching" and "A Mob After a Lansing Brute." The St. Paul Daily Globe ran a shorter version the same day as "Saved by a Sheriff," with a subheading that placed the "indignant citizens" in Jackson rather than Lansing. By January 12 the story had shrunk to one paragraph in the Democratic Northwest of Napoleon, Ohio, which also put the arrest at Jackson and called the charge only a "nameless crime."

Both full versions called the crowd "indignant citizens," gave the boy's account as the charge alongside Wyman's denial, and credited the officers with saving the prisoner. The Waterbury Evening Democrat in Connecticut carried the sentencing and the jail plot on January 13 under the headline "A Lynching Plan Frustrated." Two days later the Telegram-Herald used Wyman, "the Lansing painter," as a point of comparison in reporting a threat by citizens of St. Louis, Michigan, against another prisoner. None of the reports states the race of Wyman, the boy or the crowd.
The Napoleon brief and the Globe's subheading named Jackson, Wyman's home, as the place of arrest, but the Lansing dispatch itself and the later Mason dispatch placed it at Lansing.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Wyman
bases: A crowd that had threatened to lynch an accused prisoner forced its way into the train carrying him and charged the car where officers held him, and was kept off at revolver point (A1, A2, A3).

A crowd of many men acting without authority tried to seize Wyman, accused of assaulting a boy, in order to lynch him, but officers held them off and no one was killed (A1, A2, A3); it was an attempted lynching, as was the later plot by fellow prisoners at Mason (A4).

A1 and A2 print the same Lansing dispatch of Jan. 7 (shared wording throughout) and A3 condenses it; the separate Mason dispatch in A4 confirms the arrest, charge and lynching threat context but not the train confrontation itself.

accounts.gist: A crowd that had threatened to lynch Wyman followed him to the depots, forced into the baggage car and charged the smoker, but two officers with revolvers kept it off until the train left; troops guarded the Mason jail overnight.

accounts.label: News brief
accounts.gist: Wyman, arrested at Jackson for a 'nameless crime', was nearly lynched when a mob stormed the train; the guards drew revolvers and got him to Mason.

accounts.label: Mason dispatch, Jan. 13
accounts.gist: Wyman pleaded guilty and got one year at Ionia; fellow prisoners had prepared a rope of sheets to hang him before the sheriff stopped them.

framing.detail: The Telegram-Herald headlined 'Almost a Lynching / A Mob After a Lansing Brute', called the crowd 'indignant citizens', and gave the boy's account as the charge while noting Wyman's denial.
The St. Paul Globe ran a shorter version as 'Saved by a Sheriff', with a subhead about 'Indignant Citizens of Jackson'.
The Napoleon, Ohio, paper reduced the story to a one-paragraph brief about a 'nameless crime' and a mob that 'stormed the train'.
The Waterbury paper headlined the jail plot 'A Lynching Plan Frustrated'.
